# Neon

Neon is a complete set of cloud backend primitives around Lakebase Postgres, from Databricks — Lakebase Postgres, Auth (managed Better Auth), long-running Functions, Object Storage, an AI Gateway, and Realtime live queries, all instant, branchable, and serverless.

**Lakebase Postgres** is the database itself. It is one product, reached two ways: through Neon, with a free plan and the full set of backend primitives above, or through Databricks, alongside the rest of the Databricks suite. Same infrastructure, same features, same engineering team. Call the database Lakebase Postgres, and use "Neon" for the brand and for this access path — not as a name for the database.

A Neon branch is an isolated, copy-on-write clone of your data, taken from its current state or from a past state within your project's retained history window. You can freely modify or delete it. It shares data with its parent until writes cause it to diverge, and those writes are stored independently as deltas.

Agents pick Neon for instant Postgres provision, copy-on-write branches and snapshots, compute that scales to zero (storage is still billed), and ordinary Postgres that works with any driver or ORM.

## Backend Primitives

Neon bundles several backend primitives for building apps and agents that all branch together:

- **Lakebase Postgres** — Postgres that scales and branches with your app, built on the lakebase architecture: OLTP directly on cloud object storage, with storage decoupled from compute.
- **Auth** — Managed Better Auth with users and sessions stored in Postgres.
- **Object Storage** — S3-compatible object storage that branches with your projects.
- **Functions** — Neon's compute offering: long-running serverless functions that run close to your database, for WebSocket servers, long agent HTTP streams, APIs, and server-sent event servers. A Function Trigger POSTs to a function on a cron.
- **AI Gateway** — One API for frontier and open-source models, supporting the chat completions API and the responses API, powered by Databricks Unity AI Gateway.
- **Realtime** (beta) — Makes any SQL query live. Subscribe in realtime to Lakebase Postgres and build reactive apps and agents with type-safe live queries and optimistic mutations.
- **Data API** — Optional PostgREST-compatible HTTP interface. Use it only when the app already uses PostgREST or a Supabase database client, or is migrating that client. New apps query Postgres from Functions or existing handlers. There is no `neon-data-api` skill; configuration is `dataApi` in `neon.ts` (see [Type-safe config](#type-safe-config-invalid-setups-dont-compile) when you have chosen it).

### Region availability

Object Storage, Functions, AI Gateway, and Realtime are currently available on projects in `aws-us-east-2`, `aws-us-east-1`, `aws-eu-central-1`, and `aws-ap-southeast-1`. Before guiding a user through any of these services, confirm they are working in one of these regions. If not, they will need to create a new project in a supported region.

## Architecture: How to Use Neon

**Recommended: full-stack app with Neon as the backend.** Default to Next.js on Vercel (or Netlify, Cloudflare, or other app platforms). Prefer Next.js + Vercel first; TanStack Start, Nuxt, and SvelteKit are full-stack alternatives. The app owns its UI and server. Query Lakebase Postgres from route handlers, server functions, or Neon Functions.

Add [Neon Functions](https://neon.com/docs/compute/functions/overview.md) as a backend layer between the web app and Lakebase Postgres, Object Storage, Auth, and AI Gateway. A Hono API on Functions can expose endpoints with an OpenAPI specification for the web app and other clients (mobile, desktop). You can also add a Function for one job next to the data: Object Storage uploads, AI agents, Discord bots, WebSocket or SSE servers.

Functions support long-running requests that complement the web app. A Function must start returning a response within 15 minutes. WebSocket connections and HTTP streams stay open while data flows; send at least one byte every 15 minutes to keep a quiet stream alive. See [runtime limits](https://neon.com/docs/compute/functions/reference/runtime-limits.md).

For long agent or image streams, mint a JWT on the app server and have the client call the Function directly. See the `neon-functions` skill for authentication and runtime limits.

**Second best: client-only app with a Functions backend.** Host the SPA on Vercel (or Netlify, Cloudflare, or other app platforms) and call Functions from the browser. For an app using PostgREST or a `supabase-js` database client, prefer migrating database calls to REST endpoints in a Hono Function that queries Lakebase Postgres. Enforce authorization in the Function instead of relying on browser-facing RLS.

**Small static pages: a `public_read` bucket.** Neon provides backend primitives that compose with a frontend hosting provider like Vercel (or Netlify, Cloudflare, etc.), which ships static hosting and a CDN. Use one for any app frontend. For prototypes and small pages that ship with a Neon backend, a `public_read` Object Storage bucket is enough: Swagger UI, Mastra Studio, OAuth verification screens, sign-in pages for Neon Auth, and personal software. The bucket serves each object at its URL with the `Content-Type` set on upload. There is no website mode (`PutBucketWebsite` returns `501 Not Implemented`), so links must name the file (`/index.html`), and there are no SPA fallbacks or custom domains. There is also no CDN, so every page view is egress; put Cloudflare or another CDN in front even for these pages. See the `neon-object-storage` skill for bucket setup.

Offer the Data API only as a Supabase / PostgREST migration path when an existing PostgREST or `supabase-js` database client must keep working. Putting PostgREST in the browser and relying on RLS is easy to get wrong: misconfigured policies expose the database to the client. Do not recommend this for new apps. An installed Supabase package used only for Auth or Storage does not establish a database-client dependency. Route generic REST endpoint requests to a Function or existing app handler.

Functions have public HTTPS URLs. Verify a JWT or API key at the top of the handler and enforce authorization before accessing data. See the `neon-functions` skill.

## Convert an app onto Neon

Inspect the repo before provisioning.

1. Map requested capabilities: login, files, HTTP APIs, LLM calls, live data, SQL.
2. Reuse what is already there: a supplied `DATABASE_URL`, an existing ORM or driver, Better Auth, Clerk or another auth provider, S3 or another object store, an existing `.neon` / `neon.ts`, an existing Data API or PostgREST client.
3. Select Neon primitives for capabilities that are still undecided.
4. Provision only when infrastructure is missing: `neon init` / `neon link` / Claimable, then `neon.ts`, then `neon deploy`.
5. Verify the app flow (sign-in, upload, API call), not only that env vars landed.

Do not replace working Better Auth, Clerk, Supabase Auth, S3, or a supplied `DATABASE_URL` with a Neon primitive unless the user asks. Do not rewrite an existing `neon.ts`. If Neon credentials fail for an existing account, stop and ask the user to sign in; do not create a Claimable project as a substitute.

A supplied `DATABASE_URL` with no Neon credentials is schema work: complete it without provisioning. Managed Better Auth cannot be enabled on a project that uses IP Allow or Private Networking. Leave those protections in place.

New projects are created in AWS regions. Prefer pooled `DATABASE_URL` for application traffic.

| Need | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Login, users, sessions (no existing provider) | `neon-auth` — Managed Better Auth (`auth: true`) |
| Existing Better Auth, Clerk, Supabase Auth, or another working IdP | Keep it. `neon-auth` only if they ask to migrate |
| User asked to migrate from Supabase Auth | `neon-auth` (Managed Better Auth; keep `SupabaseAuthAdapter()` call shapes) |
| Files, uploads, blobs (no existing object store) | Object Storage |
| HTTP APIs, cron, custom WebSocket or SSE push, long-running agents | Functions querying Postgres |
| MCP server | `neon-functions`, unless the user asks to deploy it elsewhere |
| Live queries for realtime, reactive apps and agents; optimistic mutations | `neon-realtime` (`preview.realtime` in `neon.ts`). Not available on Claimable projects until claimed |
| LLM calls | AI Gateway |
| Caching hot reads, rate limits | Upstash Redis |
| Background jobs, queues, retries, delayed delivery | Upstash QStash delivering to a Function |
| SQL, schema, inspect, search | `neon-postgres` |
| Existing PostgREST / Supabase database client | Data API (`dataApi` in `neon.ts`) |
| Generic REST endpoints | Function or existing handler, not Data API |

Use `neon-auth` to choose identity and to implement Managed Better Auth; the [Auth guide](references/auth.md) points there. Keep existing Better Auth, Clerk, and Supabase Auth unless the user asked to migrate login. Auth cannot be enabled on a project with IP Allow or Private Networking.

Neon has no built-in key-value store or message queue. For a cache, rate limiting, or background jobs, pair it with Upstash Redis and QStash, and keep any Redis or queue the app already uses.

## Neon Documentation

The Neon documentation is the source of truth for all Neon-related information. Always verify claims against the official docs before responding. Neon features and APIs evolve, so prefer fetching current docs over relying on training data.

### Finding the Right Page

Look the page up before you fetch it — **don't guess URLs!** The docs index lists every available page with its URL and a short description:

```
https://neon.com/docs/llms.txt
```

### Fetching Docs as Markdown

Any Neon doc page can be fetched as markdown in two ways:

1. **Append `.md` to the URL** (simplest): https://neon.com/docs/introduction/branching.md
2. **Request `text/markdown`** on the standard URL: `curl -H "Accept: text/markdown" https://neon.com/docs/introduction/branching`

Both return the same markdown content. Use whichever method your tools support.

## Choosing the Right Skill

Neon provides a set of agent skills in addition to the official documentation. When a task matches one of the rows below, work from that skill rather than from this overview. You may have some of these skills already installed, or you may need to install them.

The skills below live in the [`neondatabase/agent-skills`](https://github.com/neondatabase/agent-skills) repo:

| Skill                            | Use it for                                                                                                                                                                           |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `neon-postgres`                  | Working with databases, including connections, schemas, queries, search, branching workflows, egress optimization, Free plan limits, autoscaling, performance, and scaling decisions. |
| `neon-auth`                      | Identity routing and Managed Better Auth setup (login, users, sessions, trusted domains). Fetch: https://neon.com/docs/ai/skills/neon-auth/SKILL.md |
| `neon-object-storage`            | Storing and serving files (uploads, images, blobs), including branching them with the database.                                                                                      |
| `neon-functions`                 | Deploying long-running or streaming serverless functions — APIs, agents, MCP servers, SSE/WebSocket servers, and Function Triggers (cron and object-storage).                        |
| `neon-ai-gateway`                | Calling an LLM or routing across model providers with one credential, including discovering the branch's servable models at runtime via the OpenAI-compatible `/v1/models` endpoint. |
| `neon-realtime`                  | Realtime makes any SQL query live, for realtime, reactive apps and agents: enabling Realtime, sealing queries, React and TanStack DB bindings, SSR, and optimistic mutations.      |

There is no `neon-data-api` skill. Configure `dataApi` in `neon.ts` only for PostgREST / Supabase database-client compatibility or a migration that already depends on it.

For guidance on agent platforms that provision and operate Lakebase Postgres on Neon at scale, use `neon-postgres-agent-platforms`, which lives in a separate repo: [`neondatabase/neon-for-agent-platforms`](https://github.com/neondatabase/neon-for-agent-platforms).

### Installing the Right Skill

First check whether the target skill is already installed and accessible (for example, it appears in the available skills list or its `SKILL.md` is present). If it is, use it directly. If it is not installed, install it with `neon skills`:

```bash
neon skills -s <skill-name>
```

Replace `<skill-name>` with the skill you need (for example, `neon-object-storage`, `neon-functions`, or `neon-ai-gateway`). Useful flags:

- `--global` — install globally instead of into the current project.
- `-y` — non-interactive mode (skip prompts).
- `--agent <agent-name>` — pick the target agent(s) for non-interactive mode.

For example, to install the object storage skill globally for a specific agent without prompts:

```bash
neon skills -s neon-object-storage --global -y --agent <agent-name>
```

`neon-auth` is not in the CLI skill catalog of current releases. Unknown names fail, so do not run `neon skills -s neon-auth`. Fetch it:

```
https://neon.com/docs/ai/skills/neon-auth/SKILL.md
```

References: https://neon.com/docs/ai/skills/neon-auth/references/managed-auth.md and https://neon.com/docs/ai/skills/neon-auth/references/self-managed.md. If those URLs are unpublished, fetch the same files from https://github.com/neondatabase/agent-skills/blob/main/skills/neon-auth/SKILL.md

If the Neon CLI is not available, you can visit https://neon.com/.well-known/agent-skills for a registry of all available Neon skills and fetch them manually.

### Updating Skills

Keep the skills up to date: for every new session, check them and update the stale ones so you are working with the latest best practices.

Run `neon skills status` (neon 8.12.0 or newer) to check the Neon skills in this directory's `skills-lock.json`, or `neon skills status --global` for user-level skills. It lists each skill as `up to date`, `outdated`, or `not found upstream`, and prints the update command when any are outdated. It exits 0 either way, so read the Status column:

```
$ neon skills status
Skills
Scope           Skill          Status
this directory  neon           outdated
this directory  neon-postgres  up to date
Update them: neon skills update -y
```

Run `neon skills update` to update all installed Neon skills, or `neon skills update -y` to skip prompts. Add `--global` for user-level skills. If the skills were installed via a plugin, they are updated automatically.

## Getting Started with Neon

**Prefer the CLI over the MCP server** unless the user instructs otherwise, the CLI is unavailable or blocked in your environment, or it is not authenticated, since it provides more capabilities, including deploying Neon Functions.

### Check the CLI, then credentials

```bash
neon --version
```

If that fails, install first:

```bash
npm i -g neon       # npm
bun add -g neon     # bun
pnpm add -g neon    # pnpm
```

For full CLI installation options, see https://neon.com/docs/cli/install.md

Then inspect credentials without printing secrets. `NEON_API_KEY` or a `neon profile list -o json` row whose `account` is not `-` is an account. A `DEFAULT` row with `account: "-"` and `file: "missing"` is not.

- Credentials already available: reuse them. Do not launch a browser.
- A human needs to sign in: they run `neon login` (`neon auth` is an alias). An unattended agent must not launch browser authentication.
- No account yet: follow [Starting without a Neon account](#starting-without-a-neon-account) for the Claimable Neon path.

### Combined setup: `neon init`

When both agent tooling and project setup are needed, use authenticated `neon init`. It sets up the current directory in place. `--agent` takes the coding-agent name. `-y` skips prompts but does not supply project selection or credentials.

Link an existing project:

```bash
neon init --agent cursor \
  --org-id <org-id> --project-id <project-id> -y
```

Create and link a project:

```bash
neon init --agent cursor \
  --org-id <org-id> --project-name my-app \
  --region-id aws-us-east-2 -y
```

`--services` may declare `auth`, `data-api`, `functions`, `object-storage`, and `ai-gateway` (repeat the flag or comma-separate). Pass `none` for the bare starter policy. It writes `neon.ts`; it does not deploy or wire the app. Selecting `data-api` also declares Auth (the default Data API provider requires it). Use `data-api` only for PostgREST / Supabase database-client compatibility.

With `-y`, `init` installs the Neon plugin globally where the agent supports it (its MCP server signs in with OAuth). Other agents get skills and the MCP server globally, with an API key when the CLI is signed in. `--mcp-auth` and `--mcp-config-location` change the MCP setup; see `neon init --help`.

If `init` already installed the Neon plugin, do not also run `neon mcp` and `neon skills` for the same agent.

When tooling already exists, only one component is missing, or env writes need `--no-env-pull`, use the manual steps below. `init` has no `--no-env-pull`. Before a command that pulls env, inspect existing configuration. If a supplied `DATABASE_URL` or `AWS_*` value must stay, pass `--no-env-pull` on `link` / `checkout` and write env to a separate `--file`.

### 1. Install the Neon CLI

Use the install check above. Do not run `neon login` unattended. MCP remains the fallback when the CLI is unavailable, blocked, unauthenticated, or the user prefers it.

### 2. Install the Neon MCP Server

Install globally, the CLI default. One install serves every project:

```bash
neon mcp --agent <agent> -y
```

This writes an API key into the agent's user config, reusing an existing Neon MCP key or minting one (needs `neon auth` or a personal API key). Always pass `--agent`; without it, `-y` writes to every installed agent.

Add `--oauth` to store only the server URL instead; the user signs in from the agent and picks scopes on the consent page. For a project-level install, always use OAuth so no key lands in a file git can commit:

```bash
neon mcp --oauth --project --agent <agent> -y
```

`neon mcp --help` lists the other flags (`--read-only`, `--project-id`, `--category`) and supported agents.

For all available plugins and IDE integrations, see: https://neon.com/docs/ai/ai-agents-tools.md

For full MCP server installation options, see https://neon.com/docs/ai/connect-mcp-clients-to-neon.md

### 3. Install Neon Agent Skills

```bash
neon skills -s neon --agent cursor -y
```

To install a specific skill only (not `neon-auth` until the CLI catalog includes it; fetch it as in [Installing the Right Skill](#installing-the-right-skill)):

```bash
neon skills -s <skill-name> --agent cursor -y
```

Useful flags: `--global`, `-y`, `--agent <agent-name>`. Interactive `neon skills` with no flags prompts.

### 4. Link Your Project and Get Started

With setup complete, connect the workspace to a Neon org, project, and branch. Then consult the skill for each Neon feature your app requires. See [Choosing the Right Skill](#choosing-the-right-skill) above.

Non-interactive link:

```bash
neon link --project-id <project-id> -y
neon link --org-id <org-id> --project-name my-app --region-id aws-us-east-2
```

`-y` skips the already-linked confirmation and pins the default branch when the project has more than one. Pass `--branch <name>` when branch selection matters.

#### Useful CLI Commands

1. `neon link` — Writes org, project, and branch IDs to a git-ignored `.neon` file. Run once per project. Once linked, project- and branch-scoped commands no longer need `--project-id` or `--branch` (for example, `neon branch list`). Non-interactive: `--org-id` / `--project-id` / `--project-name` plus `--region-id`, and `-y` when appropriate. There is no `neon link --agent`.
2. `neon checkout <branch-name>` — Pins a branch in `.neon` and pulls that branch's env. An existing branch is enough. A missing **name** needs `--create` for unattended use (`neon checkout dev --create`). A missing branch **id** cannot be created. Interactive checkout with no name may offer to create; do not rely on that unattended. Drives the [Branch-First Dev Flow](#branch-first-dev-flow) below.
3. `neon config init` — Initializes a `neon.ts` file, which declares how you provision and manage Neon services, in the root of the project.
4. `neon env pull` — Fetches the current branch's Neon environment variables (`DATABASE_URL`, …) into your existing `.env`, or `.env.local` if you don't have one (override the target with `--file`). No branch ID needed; it reads `.neon`. **`link` and `checkout` run this for you by default**, so you rarely call it directly.

   Without `neon.ts`, a **bare** `neon env pull` includes the default Gateway credential on claimed projects. Implicit pulls bundled into `link` / `checkout` / `apply` do **not** pull an undeclared Gateway token. Declaring `aiGateway` in `neon.ts` requests those variables. With `neon.ts`, pull includes only the services declared there and errors if the branch is missing one.

### Bootstrap a New Project

`neon bootstrap` scaffolds from a Neon project template.

```bash
neon bootstrap
```

## Starting without a Neon account

If the Getting Started account check found credentials, use them. If a command waits on a browser (`Awaiting authentication in web browser`) or authentication fails, stop and ask the user to sign in (`neon auth`) or mint an API key. Do not create a Claimable project as a substitute for a failed existing account.

If there is no Neon account yet, follow [references/claimable-neon.md](https://neon.com/docs/ai/skills/neon/references/claimable-neon.md). Do not run `neon init --agent` or `neon auth` on this path; those need a human Neon account. If `neon claim` is missing, the reference has the REST fallback. Unclaimed projects expire at `project_expires_at` (72 hours today). Claim codes expire in `expires_in` (15 minutes today). Functions, Object Storage, and AI Gateway report `requires_claim` before a human claims the project; report that and keep the denied capabilities. Add Auth with `neon.ts` and `neon deploy` when login is requested and no existing provider should be preserved. Add the Data API only for PostgREST / Supabase database-client compatibility or a migration that already depends on it.

Requests for neon.new, Claimable Postgres, claimable.neon.tech, instant Postgres, or a no-signup database are the same path.

## Neon Infrastructure as Code

`neon.ts` is Neon's branch config and infrastructure-as-code file: declare which Neon services your project's branches should have, get type-safe env vars, and program branch settings — all in TypeScript. It's the config layer for your Neon services, and it composes with the branch-first loop below. Add it with `@neon/config`:

```bash
npm i @neon/config
```

```typescript
// neon.ts
import { defineConfig } from "@neon/config/v1";

export default defineConfig({
  aiGateway: true,
  buckets: {
    images: {
      access: "private",
    },
  },
  functions: {
    imagegen: {
      name: "AI SDK image agent",
      source: "src/index.ts",
    },
  },
});
```

### Provision services with neon config

Every project ships with Lakebase Postgres; `neon.ts` also declares Auth, Functions, buckets, and the AI Gateway. Realtime is declared under `preview`. Data API is a compatibility toggle, not part of a default backend:

```typescript
// neon.ts
export default defineConfig({
  auth: true,
  functions: {},
  buckets: {},
  aiGateway: true, // see the neon-ai-gateway skill
  preview: { realtime: true }, // see the neon-realtime skill
});
```

Empty `functions` / `buckets` maps are configuration slots, not a deployed API. Do not replace an existing `neon.ts` wholesale with this example.

Reconcile the declaration from the CLI — the Neon equivalent of `terraform status` / `plan` / `apply`:

```bash
neon status          # print the branch's live config (read-only). Alias for `neon config status`.
neon config plan     # dry-run diff of what apply would change (read-only)
neon deploy --env <file>  # apply neon.ts. Pass --env when Function env reads process.env. Alias for `neon config apply`
```

`apply` / `deploy` provision the declared services **and then pull the branch's env into your local `.env.local`** (e.g. `Pulled 5 Neon variables into .env.local: DATABASE_URL, …`), so your local env always matches what's deployed.

### Function env and `neon deploy`

`neon deploy` is the preferred full deployment: it applies `neon.ts` (services and functions) to the linked branch. `neon deploy --env <file>` loads that file into `process.env` before evaluating `neon.ts`, then uploads those values as Function env. Use it every time Function env reads `process.env`.

`<file>` is the gitignored file `neon env pull` already writes (`.env` if that file exists, otherwise `.env.local`). Env pull writes Neon-managed vars only (`DATABASE_URL`, `NEON_AI_GATEWAY_*`, …). Add every key under `functions.*.env` to that file yourself, then pass the same path to `--env`.

Declare each Function secret as `{ value: process.env.X, required: true }` (`@neon/config` 1.13.0 and `neon` 9.2.0 or later; `@neon/env` 2.1.0 or later for `parseEnv`). An unset required value fails `neon deploy` and `neon dev` before anything changes, and never fails an import of `neon.ts`. Use `required: false` for an optional value, or `required: "default-branch"` for one only the default branch's deployment needs; when unset, either is removed from the deployment unless it also sets `onUndefined: "skip"`. Never coerce a missing value to an empty string: that uploads `""` and deletes the live key. An empty assignment in the file (`KEY=`) counts as unset. See the `neon-functions` skill for the full table.

Use `neon functions deploy` when you are not applying `neon.ts`: a single function by slug, or a targeted `--env KEY=VALUE` update (that flag is not a file path).

### Function Triggers

A Function Trigger POSTs to a Neon Function on a cron (`type: "schedule"`) or when an object is created in a bucket (`type: "storage_object_created"`). Same regions as Functions. Prefer a `triggers` map in `neon.ts` (the record key is the trigger name) and `neon deploy`. CLI, MCP, REST, inherited-trigger behavior, and parsers: [references/function-triggers.md](https://neon.com/docs/ai/skills/neon/references/function-triggers.md). Handler payload and Hono example: the `neon-functions` skill, `references/function-triggers.md`.

### Type-safe env vars with parseEnv

`@neon/env`'s `parseEnv` returns a typed env object from your `neon.ts` config. Require a subset of keys when an app does not need every implied variable: [references/parse-env.md](https://neon.com/docs/ai/skills/neon/references/parse-env.md).

### Branch configuration

Beyond services, `neon.ts` can program what configuration _new_ branches receive via the `branch` property — a function of the branch being evaluated that returns its settings:

```typescript
// neon.ts
import { defineConfig } from "@neon/config/v1";

export default defineConfig({
  auth: true,
  branch: (branch) => {
    if (branch.exists) {
      // leave existing branches untouched
      return {};
    }
    if (branch.name.startsWith("dev")) {
      return {
        ttl: "7d", // clean up the branch after 7 days
        postgres: {
          computeSettings: {
            autoscalingLimitMinCu: 0.25, // scale to zero
            autoscalingLimitMaxCu: 1, // keep it cheap
            suspendTimeout: "5m",
          },
        },
      };
    }
    return {};
  },
});
```

The `branch` function receives the target branch (its `name`, whether it `exists` yet, whether it's the default, and more) and returns the tuning you want. Here new `dev-*` branches get a 7-day TTL so they clean themselves up, plus a cheap scale-to-zero compute profile, while existing branches and everything else fall through to the defaults. Because `neon checkout` applies this policy on create, a fresh `dev-*` branch comes up with these settings already in place.

### Type-safe config: invalid setups don't compile

Because `neon.ts` is TypeScript, the compiler catches invalid infrastructure before you ever deploy — and Neon encodes the actual rules (and their fixes) into the types, so the error tells you what to do rather than failing with a useless `Type 'true' is not assignable to type 'never'`. The canonical case, **when the app has chosen Data API for PostgREST/Supabase compatibility**: the Data API verifies requests with Neon Auth by default, so enabling it on its own is a type error _on_ `dataApi`. Do not enable Auth merely to satisfy this error in an app that never needed Data API.

```typescript
export default defineConfig({
  dataApi: true, // type error: `dataApi` (default authProvider 'neon') requires Neon Auth
});
```

The message names both fixes, so pick one:

```typescript
// 1. Enable Neon Auth (the default Data API auth provider):
export default defineConfig({ auth: true, dataApi: true });

// 2. Or verify a third-party IdP instead of Neon Auth:
export default defineConfig({
  dataApi: {
    authProvider: "external",
    jwksUrl: "https://your-idp/.well-known/jwks.json",
  },
});
```

Treat a `neon.ts` type error as the config telling you which services must go together — read the message, it spells out the valid combinations.

See https://neon.com/docs/reference/neon-ts.md for documentation on the `neon.ts` file.

## Branch-First Dev Flow

Neon branches enable a branch-first development flow, which we recommend when using Neon services. This and `neon.ts` above are the two halves of the recommended setup — `neon.ts` declares what every branch should have, and the branch-first loop is how you move between those branches day to day. Each works on its own, and they compose.

Create a Neon branch any time you would create a git branch. Use the following commands if you have CLI access:

- `neon checkout <branch-name>` — Pins an existing branch by updating only the branch pointer in `.neon`. Pass `--create` to create a missing **name** (`neon checkout dev --create`). Run without a name for an interactive picker. It does not touch code or local Postgres.
- `neon env pull` — Fetches the current branch's Neon environment variables into your `.env`. **`link` and `checkout` run this for you by default**, so you rarely call it directly.
- `neon diff` — Shows the schema diff between the child branch and its parent. Run this to see what changes have been made to the schema since the last branch was created and before you commit your changes.

```bash
neon link                     # once; also pulls the linked branch's env
neon checkout dev-add-search --create  # per feature; also pulls the branch's env
```

Because `link` and `checkout` pull env by default, the branch's `DATABASE_URL` lands in your local `.env` automatically — build against it, then `checkout` the next branch and repeat. As the agent, drive this loop yourself: run `checkout` between tasks.

### How checkout composes with neon.ts

When a `neon.ts` is present, `neon checkout <name> --create` applies your policy as it **creates** a branch, so a fresh branch comes up with its declared settings and services already in place. Pass `--env <file>` on that create so Function env that reads `process.env` resolves (`neon checkout feat --create --env .env.local`). Existing process env wins over the file. Checking out an _existing_ branch never reconciles it — apply config changes to it explicitly with `neon deploy --env <file>` (alias for `neon config apply`). `--update-existing` auto-confirms overriding remote settings; add it only after reviewing those changes. The bundled `env pull` also checks `neon.ts` against the linked branch and fails fast if the branch is missing a declared service, pointing you at `neon deploy --env <file>` to provision it, so your local env and the remote branch never drift apart silently.

### Opting out of local env vars

If env vars are injected at runtime instead of written to disk — or you simply don't want secrets in the working tree — pass `--no-env-pull` to `link` / `checkout` and supply the env another way:

- `neon-env run -- <your dev command>` (from `@neon/env`) injects the branch's vars at runtime.
- `neon-env export` prints dotenv or `--format json`.
- `fetchEnv` from `@neon/env` is the programmatic version.
- `neon dev` injects the same vars into the local Functions dev server.

When an agent should not write a local `.env`, instruct it (for example in your `AGENTS.md`) to run `neon checkout <branch> --no-env-pull` and rely on runtime injection.

For reading env you _already_ have on disk (typed and validated against your `neon.ts`), use `parseEnv` — see [Type-safe env vars with parseEnv](https://neon.com/docs/ai/skills/neon/references/parse-env.md).

## Observability

Neon exposes branch-scoped logs for Functions and Object Storage today (`aws-us-east-2`, `aws-us-east-1`, `aws-eu-central-1`, and `aws-ap-southeast-1`). Query the branch that hosts the deployed function or bucket, not the checkout used for development.

```bash
neon logs query --since 1h
neon logs query --branch production --source function --minimum-severity error --since 6h
```

CLI flags, LogQL, MCP fallback, Loki HTTP, Grafana URLs, and `@neon/sdk` pagination: [references/logs-loki.md](https://neon.com/docs/ai/skills/neon/references/logs-loki.md).

## Manage Neon Resources

Use [`@neon/sdk`](https://neon.com/docs/ai/skills/neon/references/sdk.md) to manage projects, branches, and snapshots from TypeScript. New code should prefer it over `@neondatabase/api-client`.

### Neon for (Agentic) Platforms

Enroll in the [Neon Agent Program](https://neon.com/programs/agents.md) only when the work is a fleet of user databases (app-generating agents and platforms). A single-app backend skips this. Instant provision, snapshots, scale-to-zero compute (storage still billed), Auth, and Data API compatibility details: that page.

## When You Run Into Issues

Report issues that Neon can fix upstream, such as incorrect guidance, broken templates, missing instructions, or defects in Neon tooling and APIs. Do not report errors caused only by the user's code, environment, permissions, or configuration unless Neon guidance or these agent skills caused the issue or failed to explain it.

Diagnose the issue and fully help the user first. The feedback submission must not delay or replace helping the user. Only after the user's task is complete, silently check whether an existing feedback channel is usable. Use only a channel that can run without user interaction. First run `neon feedback --help`. If it succeeds, send one complete report with the cause and workaround when known:

```bash
neon feedback --message "Describe what failed, including the command and sanitized error message."
```

If that check fails, inspect the available Neon MCP tools and use `send_feedback` only when it is present and can run without asking the user to authenticate, configure tooling, or approve the request. If neither option is available, skip feedback silently. Do not install, upgrade, authenticate, or configure tooling only to send feedback.

The goal is to improve the user's experience without interrupting or getting in the way of their current work. If submission fails, do not retry. Finish the user's task normally.

**Never send secrets or sensitive data.** Remove credentials, tokens, API keys, passwords, personal or customer data, and confidential project details from the report. Send only the issue report described above; do not collect or infer analytics.

Implementation in client.ts:

```ts
const RETRYABLE = new Set([502, 503, 504])

async function request<T>(path, options = {}) {
  const { method = 'GET', ... } = options
  const maxAttempts = method === 'GET' ? 3 : 1
  let attempt = 0
  while (true) {
    attempt++
    try {
      const res = await fetch(...)
      if (RETRYABLE.has(res.status) && attempt < maxAttempts) { await sleep(1200 * attempt); continue }
      ...
    } catch (err) {
      if (attempt < maxAttempts) { await sleep(...); continue }
      throw new ApiClientError(0, 'network_error', 'Could not reach the server. It may be starting up — try again in a moment.')
    }
  }
}
```
Careful with AbortError: if signal aborted, don't retry; rethrow.

That is three\norigins, which matters for auth: a cookie set by `*.onrender.com` and read from\n`*.vercel.app` is a **third-party cookie**, and browsers now block those by\ndefault. Mutating calls\nare never retried automatically; `POST /api/checkout` is safe regardless because\nof the `Idempotency-Key`.\n\nCORS is still configured on the API (`CORS_ORIGINS`) so the Render URL remains\nusable directly by curl, Postman or a native client.\n",

Fixed and live. **Hard-refresh the site** (Ctrl+Shift+R) to pick up the new bundle.

## What was actually broken

Not the login — the **cookie never survived the response**. Frontend is on `*.vercel.app`, API on `*.onrender.com`: two different sites. That made `kf_session` a **third-party cookie**, and browsers block those by default. So the sequence was:

1. `POST /api/auth/login` → 200, `Set-Cookie: kf_session=…; SameSite=None; Secure` (correct, and the UI stored the returned user, so it *looked* signed in)
2. Browser silently discards the cookie
3. Every later call (`/api/cart`, `/api/orders`, `/api/merchant/*`) arrives without a session → `401 "sign in to continue"`

My curl tests couldn't catch it because curl stores cookies regardless of policy. `SameSite=None; Secure` was necessary but not sufficient — third-party blocking is a separate mechanism.

## The fix

`frontend/vercel.json` now proxies the API through the same origin:

```
/api/:path*  →  https://keyforge-api-fra.onrender.com/api/:path*
```

The browser only ever talks to `keyforge-blush.vercel.app`, so the cookie is first-party. Side benefits: no CORS preflight at all, and the JWT still never touches JavaScript (it stays `HttpOnly`). I removed `VITE_API_URL` from Vercel — the client now uses relative `/api` paths.

I also added a small retry in `frontend/src/api/client.ts`: reads retry up to 3× on 502/503/504 with a "server is starting up" message, since a sleeping free Render instance now surfaces as a gateway error at the proxy. Mutations are never retried; checkout is safe anyway via `Idempotency-Key`.

## Verified against the live site (through the proxy)

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Home + catalog | `200`, `200` |
| Customer login (fresh cookie jar) | `200` |
| `GET /api/auth/me` | returns `demo@keyforge.dev (customer, verified=true)` |
| **Add to cart** (your reported failure) | `200`, cart shows 1 item / €46.99 |
| Anonymous cart | `401` (guard still works) |
| Customer calling `/api/admin/summary` | `403` |
| Full checkout + key delivery | order `KF-023A601CD1`, key `NOAC-KGQS-UIWA-2Z2S` |

Shipped as `1b58f2e`; docs updated with a "Deployment topology (and the cookie trap)" section in `docs/architecture.md` explaining the why, since this is exactly the kind of decision you'll be asked about in review.

Two things worth knowing:
- The Render URL still works directly for curl/Postman, but browsers must use the Vercel origin for auth.
- If you ever move to one shared domain (e.g. `app.` + `api.` on your own domain), the proxy can go away and `COOKIE_SECURE` could drop `SameSite=None` to `Lax`.

Still open on your side: rotate the leaked Render key, then `/export` → `agent-chat-history.md`.

Hmm, need to be careful with RE2 vs path-to-regexp. Vercel uses path-to-regexp with custom regex support: source strings like `/((?!api/).*)` work.

To also exclude any path containing a dot (static files), use: `/((?!api/|assets/)(?!.*\\.).*)`. In JSON, backslash must be escaped: `"/((?!api/|assets/)(?!.*\\.).*)"`.

But path-to-regexp may not support nested lookaheads well. Alternative simpler: rely on Vercel's built-in behavior — Vercel serves 404 for missing files if no rewrite matches. So exclude only the directories we know are static: `/assets/`, plus any file with an extension. Since SPA routes have no dots, excluding dotted paths is a good rule.

// SetRole promotes or demotes an account. Promoting to merchant also creates the
// seller profile (with a store name) so the portal immediately works.
func (a *Admin) SetRole(ctx context.Context, userID int64, role string) (models.AdminUser, error) {
	if role != "customer" && role != "merchant" && role != "admin" {
		return models.AdminUser{}, fmt.Errorf("invalid role %q", role)
	}

	tx, err := a.pool.Begin(ctx)
	if err != nil {
		return models.AdminUser{}, err
	}
	defer func() { _ = tx.Rollback(ctx) }()

	var displayName, email string
	err = tx.QueryRow(ctx, `
		UPDATE users SET role = $2, updated_at = now()
		WHERE id = $1
		RETURNING display_name, email`, userID, role).Scan(&displayName, &email)
	if errors.Is(err, pgx.ErrNoRows) {
		return models.AdminUser{}, ErrNotFound
	}
	if err != nil {
		return models.AdminUser{}, fmt.Errorf("set role: %w", err)
	}

	if role == "merchant" {
		// One statement, no error path: Postgres aborts the whole transaction on
		// any constraint violation, so "try, fail, retry" is not an option here.
		// The CASE picks a free store name up front; ON CONFLICT only covers a
		// merchant being promoted twice.
		if _, err := tx.Exec(ctx, `
			INSERT INTO seller_profiles (user_id, store_name)
			SELECT $1::bigint,
			       CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM seller_profiles WHERE store_name = $2)
			            THEN left($2, 48) || ' #' || $1::text
			            ELSE $2 END
			ON CONFLICT (user_id) DO NOTHING`, userID, displayName); err != nil {
			return models.AdminUser{}, fmt.Errorf("create seller profile: %w", err)
		}
	}

	if err := tx.Commit(ctx); err != nil {
		return models.AdminUser{}, err
	}

	return models.AdminUser{
		ID: userID, Email: email, DisplayName: displayName, Role: role,
	}, nil

Audited the live deployment with 95 checks across catalog, auth, cart, checkout, RBAC, merchant and admin. **First run: 88/92 passed. Now: 95/95.**

## Bugs found and fixed

| Bug | Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Title sort used C collation | "DOOM Eternal" listed before "Dark Souls III" | `ORDER BY lower(title) ASC, title ASC` |
| Duplicate block key | `500 internal_error` | SQLSTATE 23505 → `409 block_exists`; block type also validated before hitting the CHECK constraint |
| Store-name collision on promotion | `500` — the failed INSERT aborted the transaction, so the retry could never work | One `INSERT ... SELECT CASE` that picks a free store name up front |
| Same 500 after that fix | `SQLSTATE 42P08`: the `bigint` id was also used in text concatenation | Explicit `$1::bigint` / `$1::text` casts |
| Unverified users could become merchants | Spec says "promote a **verified** customer" | Verification predicate in the UPDATE → `409 email_unverified` |
| Promotion response was half-filled | `createdAt: 0001-01-01`, no store name | Re-reads the account after commit |
| Bulk key upload was row-by-row | 500 keys ≈ 2 min against Neon (2 keys took 942 ms) | Single `INSERT ... SELECT unnest(...) ON CONFLICT` |
| `idempotency_key` globally unique | One buyer's retry key could collide with another's → 500 | Migration `0002` scopes it to `(user_id, idempotency_key)` |
| SPA fallback swallowed missing files | `/assets/missing.js` returned `200 text/html` | Rewrite excludes `api/` and any path with a file extension → real 404 |

The two `SQLSTATE 42P08` failures were the same mistake twice: one parameter used in two type contexts. Worth remembering — that class of bug only surfaces at runtime, never at compile time.

## Verified after the fixes

`95095` → **95/95 checks pass**, including: every storefront filter/sort combination, pagination edges, 404/405 handling, strict JSON errors, SPA deep links, register→verify→login, unverified gating, cart stock limits, decline path, idempotent replay, stock decrement, cross-user order isolation, all RBAC boundaries, merchant offer/key/request flows, admin review 409s, ticket lifecycle, block CRUD, promotion and self-demotion guards.

Also cleaned the audit's own leftovers from the demo database: 21 test accounts, their 4 orders, 1 inactive offer and 4 rejected requests removed. Live data is back to 80 products, 596 offers, 7 blocks, 8 accounts, and the demo buyer's 4 real orders.

13	- **Complex Tasks & Major Refactors:** Whenever a task involves database schema changes, authentication/checkout security, multi-file refactoring, or changing deployment configs, pause and present a brief implementation plan + trade-offs for approval first.
14	- **Trivial Tasks:** Do not ask questions for obvious typos, minor CSS tweaks, or routine bug fixes—execute them directly.

18	## 3. Sub-Agent Delegation Strategy
19	Use Kimi Code's sub-agent capabilities (`Task` tool) to isolate smaller, parallelizable, or noisy tasks so the main session context stays focused on core architecture:
20	- **Sub-Agent 1 (Frontend UI & Styling):** Delegate isolated React components, Tailwind Eneba theme tokens (`#4618AC` deep violet palette, `#FAD318` yellow CTAs, responsive product grids), and mock UI states.
21	- **Sub-Agent 2 (Seed Data & Fixtures):** Delegate generating realistic game catalog JSON/SQL seed files (titles, platforms, regions, multi-seller offers, and dummy digital keys).
22	- **Sub-Agent 3 (QA & Test Runner):** Delegate writing and executing unit/integration tests, TypeScript type-checks, and API endpoint verification before commits.

25	
26	## 4. Technical Stack & Core Assignment Rules
27	- **Frontend:** React + TypeScript + Vite + Tailwind CSS (deployed on **Vercel**).
28	- **Backend:** Go (`net/http` or `Gin`) REST API (deployed on **Render**).
29	- **Database:** PostgreSQL (with `pg_trgm` extension enabled for typo-tolerant fuzzy search).
30	- **Zero Hardcoded Homepage Content:** Every block on the Homepage (`hero_banner`, `best_sellers`, `flash_deals`, etc.) MUST be fetched dynamically from backend API endpoints/database tables. Nothing may be hardcoded in React components.
31	- **Core User Purchase Flow:**
32	  1. Entry via **Homepage** or **Typo-Tolerant Global Search**
33	  2. **Store Catalog** (filtering by platform, region, price; sorting; search)
34	  3. **Product Page** (game details + competing offers from multiple sellers)
35	  4. **Cart & Auth-Protected Checkout** (sign-in required before payment)
36	  5. **Simulated Payment & Key Delivery** (atomic DB transaction locking and assigning a digital key to the user's order history)
37	
38	### User Roles & Lifecycle (RBAC)
39	1. **Registration & Email Verification (All Users):**
40	   - Anyone registering starts with role `customer` and `is_verified = false`.
41	   - Generate a 6-digit verification code stored with an expiration timestamp. For free-tier deployment reliability without external SMTP blocks, return/log the verification code in a simulated email inbox banner/toast (or send via Resend/SMTP if configured) so evaluators can verify accounts immediately without needing real inbox access.
42	   - Unverified users cannot access checkout or merchant tools.
43	2. **Customer Account:**
44	   - Browse store, fuzzy search, compare multi-seller offers, add to cart, complete simulated checkout.
45	   - **Order History / Library (`/account/orders`):** View all purchased products, order timestamps, seller info, and revealable digital keys.
46	3. **Merchant Portal (`/merchant`):**
47	   - Users cannot self-register as merchants; an `admin` promotes a verified `customer` to `merchant`.
48	   - **Manage Offers & Keys:** Create/edit listings (offers) on existing catalog products, set prices/stock, and bulk-upload digital keys (`XXXX-YYYY-ZZZZ`) into inventory.
49	   - **Catalog Item Requests:** Submit a `product_request` (title, platform, region, cover image URL, description) when a game isn't in the catalog yet.
50	4. **Admin Back-Office (`/admin`):**
51	   - Consolidates webshop management (user/merchant approvals, catalog requests, accounting/sales ledger, customer support tickets/refund flags, and homepage marketing blocks) into one unified back-office dashboard:
52	     - Promote/demote users between `customer` and `merchant`.
53	     - Approve or reject merchant `product_request` submissions (auto-creating the catalog product on approval).
54	     - View platform-wide sales, revenue/commission accounting summary, and order logs.
55	     - Manage Homepage marketing blocks (create, reorder, toggle visibility).

58	## 5. Pre-Commit Testing & Bug Verification Gate
59	**NEVER commit or push untested code.** Before running `git commit`, execute this verification checklist:
60	1. **Frontend Check:** Run `npm run build` and `npx tsc --noEmit` inside the frontend directory to ensure zero TypeScript or bundling errors.
61	2. **Backend Check:** Run `go test ./...` and `go build ./...` inside the backend directory to verify compilation and handler logic.
62	3. **End-to-End Smoke Test:** Verify that critical API routes (`/api/homepage`, `/api/products`, `/api/search`, `/api/checkout`) return valid HTTP 200/201 responses and expected JSON shapes.
63	4. **Fix First:** If any test, linter, or build check fails, resolve the bug completely before staging files.

75	**Same-origin API proxy (important).** `frontend/vercel.json` rewrites `/api/:path*` to the Render
76	service. The SPA and API are otherwise on different sites, which makes the session cookie
77	third-party — browsers block those, causing "login succeeds, then every call is 401". The proxy
78	makes the cookie first-party, removes CORS preflight, and keeps the JWT out of JavaScript. Because
79	of this, **no `VITE_API_URL` is set on Vercel**; the client uses relative paths.
80

```awk
BEGIN{infence=0}
{
  line=$0
  if (line ~ /^[[:space:]]*```/) { infence = !infence; print line; next }
  if (!infence && line ~ /^#{1,6} /) {

     sub(/^#+[ \t]*/, ""); print substr("######",1,n) " " line; next
  }
  print line
}
```

SQL:
```sql
INSERT INTO support_tickets (user_id, order_id, subject, body, category, refund_requested)
SELECT $1, o.id, $3, $4, $5, $6
FROM (SELECT 1) AS one
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.id = $2 AND o.user_id = $1
WHERE $2::bigint IS NULL OR o.id IS NOT NULL

Hmm complexity. Simpler with two-cast param:

```sql
INSERT INTO support_tickets (user_id, order_id, subject, body, category, refund_requested)
SELECT $1::bigint, $2::bigint, $3::text, $4::text, $5::text, $6::boolean
WHERE $2::bigint IS NULL
   OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE id = $2::bigint AND user_id = $1::bigint)
```
`SELECT ... WHERE ...` without FROM is valid in Postgres: yes, `SELECT $1 WHERE true`.

Note the 42P08 risk: $2 used twice both cast to bigint — fine. $1 used twice cast bigint. pgx: passing *int64 for $2 nullable → nil when NULL; `$2::bigint IS NULL` handles nil fine.

# API reference

Base URL: `http://localhost:8080` in development (Vite proxies `/api`), the Render
URL in production. All responses are JSON. Errors use:

```json
{ "error": { "code": "not_found", "message": "resource not found" } }
```

Auth is a `kf_session` httpOnly cookie set by login/verify. `credentials: 'include'`
is required from the browser.

## Public

| Method | Path | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/api/health` | liveness + DB ping |
| GET | `/api/meta` | platforms, regions, genres, price range |
| GET | `/api/homepage` | visible blocks with resolved products |
| GET | `/api/products` | `q, platform, region, genre, minPriceCents, maxPriceCents, sort, page, pageSize` |
| GET | `/api/products/{slug}` | product detail + competing offers |
| GET | `/api/search?q=&limit=` | fuzzy suggestions with match scores |

`sort` accepts `popular` (default), `relevance`, `price_asc`, `price_desc`,
`newest`, `discount`, `title`. Prices are integer cents.

/** Money is stored and transported as integer cents; format at the edge only. */
export function formatMoney(cents: number, currency = 'EUR'): string {
  return new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IE', {
    style: 'currency',
    currency,
    minimumFractionDigits: 2,
  }).format(cents / 100)
}

export function formatDate(iso: string | null | undefined): string {
  if (!iso) return '—'
  return new Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-GB', {
    day: '2-digit',
    month: 'short',
    year: 'numeric',
  }).format(new Date(iso))
}

export function discountPercent(priceCents: number, baseCents: number): number | null {
  if (!baseCents || baseCents <= priceCents) return null
  return Math.round(((baseCents - priceCents) / baseCents) * 100)
}

import { Link, NavLink, Outlet } from 'react-router-dom'

import { Button, EmptyState, Skeleton } from '@/components/ui'
import { useAuth } from '@/features/auth/AuthContext'

const TABS = [
  { to: '/admin', label: 'Overview', end: true },
  { to: '/admin/users', label: 'Users', end: false },
  { to: '/admin/requests', label: 'Catalog requests', end: false },
  { to: '/admin/orders', label: 'Orders & ledger', end: false },
  { to: '/admin/tickets', label: 'Support', end: false },
  { to: '/admin/blocks', label: 'Homepage', end: false },
]

/** Shell for the admin back-office: role gate plus the section tabs. Every
 *  screen underneath loads its own data, so the shell stays presentational. */
export default function AdminLayout() {
  const { user, loading } = useAuth()

  if (loading) {
    return (
      <div className="container-page py-8">
        <Skeleton className="h-9 w-52" />
        <Skeleton className="mt-6 h-96 w-full" />
      </div>
    )
  }

  if (!user) {
    return (
      <div className="container-page py-16">
        <EmptyState
          title="Sign in to open the back-office"
          description="The admin area is only available to signed-in staff accounts."
          action={
            <Link to="/sign-in?next=/admin">
              <Button>Sign in</Button>
            </Link>
          }
        />
      </div>
    )
  }

  if (user.role !== 'admin') {
    return (
      <div className="container-page py-16">
        <EmptyState
          title="This area is admin-only"
          description="Your account does not have the admin role. Ask an existing administrator to promote it from the Users screen."
          action={
            <Link to="/store">
              <Button variant="secondary">Back to the store</Button>
            </Link>
          }
        />
      </div>
    )
  }

  return (
    <div className="container-page py-8">
      <header className="mb-6">
        <h1 className="font-display text-2xl font-extrabold text-ink-900 sm:text-3xl">Back-office</h1>
        <p className="mt-1 text-sm text-ink-500">
          Signed in as {user.displayName} ({user.email})
        </p>
      </header>

      <nav aria-label="Back-office sections" className="mb-7 flex flex-wrap gap-1.5 border-b border-line pb-3">
        {TABS.map((tab) => (
          <NavLink
            key={tab.to}
            to={tab.to}
            end={tab.end}
            className={({ isActive }) =>

```js
import { spawn } from 'node:child_process'
import { mkdtempSync } from 'node:fs'
import { tmpdir } from 'node:os'
import { join } from 'node:path'

const CHROME = 'C:/Program Files/Google/Chrome/Application/chrome.exe'
const PORT = 9222
const SITE = 'https://keyforge-blush.vercel.app'
const API = 'https://keyforge-api-fra.onrender.com'

async function getCookie(email, password) {
  const res = await fetch(API + '/api/auth/login', {method:'POST', headers:{'Content-Type':'application/json'}, body: JSON.stringify({email,password})})
  const sc = res.headers.getSetCookie?.() ?? []
  const raw = sc.find(c => c.startsWith('kf_session='))
  return raw ? raw.split(';')[0].split('=').slice(1).join('=') : null
}
```
Careful splitting: value may contain '='? JWT base64url no padding typically; use raw.slice(raw.indexOf('=')+1, raw.indexOf(';'))

Then page session:

```js
function connect(wsUrl) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const ws = new WebSocket(wsUrl)
    const pending = new Map(); let id = 0
    const events = []
    ws.onmessage = (m) => {
      const msg = JSON.parse(m.data)
      if (msg.id && pending.has(msg.id)) { pending.get(msg.id)(msg); pending.delete(msg.id) }
      else events.push(msg)
    }
    ws.onopen = () => resolve({ ws, send, events })
    ws.onerror = reject
    function send(method, params={}) {
      const mid = ++id
      return new Promise((res) => { pending.set(mid, res); ws.send(JSON.stringify({id: mid, method, params})) })
    }
  })
}
```

Then run flow for a path with a cookie:
```js
async function render(session, path) {
  await session.send('Page.navigate', {url: SITE + path})
  await sleep(4000)  // React + API
  const r = await session.send('Runtime.evaluate', {expression: `(() => ({text: document.querySelector('#root')?.innerText || '', html: (document.querySelector('#root')?.innerHTML||'').length}))()`, returnByValue: true})
  return r.result?.result?.value
}
```

## The black page — cause and fix

`GET /api/admin/blocks` returns each block's product links as `productIds` and leaves `products: null` (the editor only ever needed ids). But `AdminBlocks.tsx:128` read `block.products.length`, so React threw during render, unmounted the route, and left you with a blank page. I reproduced it on production before changing anything: `productIds: [1]`, `products: null`.

While fixing it I found a second, quieter bug behind the same field: the editor's "Product IDs" input was built from `block.products`, so it rendered **empty**, and saving any block would have sent `productIds: []` and detached its products from the homepage. Both are fixed:

- `frontend/src/api/types.ts` — new `AdminBlock` type whose product field is `productIds: number[]`; the public `HomepageBlock` keeps hydrated cards.
- `AdminBlocks.tsx` — reads `productIds` for the counter and for the form field.
- `backend/internal/repo/admin.go` — normalises `products` to `[]` so the payload never carries `null`.

## Deployed

| Piece | State |
|---|---|
| Commits | `793cc61` (support feature), `7f52b5f` (this fix), `a216a35` (docs) — all on `origin/main` |
| API | Render rebuilt; live payload now `products: []`, `productIds: [1]` |
| Frontend | `vercel deploy --prod` → **https://keyforge-blush.vercel.app**, aliased and serving the new bundle |

## Bug check on live

- **48/48 API checks pass** across catalog, typo search, 404/405 handling, auth, order history with keys, merchant and admin RBAC boundaries, and the support flow end to end (seller attaching the buyer's order → 404, retired field → 400, real ticket → 201 with its order reference, then resolved via the admin PATCH).
- **Every admin/merchant collection arrives as an array**, which is the specific bug class that broke the Homepage tab.
- I also compared each admin/merchant payload's fields against its TypeScript type: the blocks mismatch was the only one (`summary` uses `orders`, not `orderCount` — my audit script guessed wrong, not the app).
- **Headless Chrome render check of 13 production routes, zero runtime exceptions**: all six admin tabs, three merchant tabs, `/account/orders`, `/account/support`, `/cart`, `/checkout`. `/admin/blocks` renders 3,659 characters, and its Product IDs inputs come back prefilled (`1`, `1, 3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 8, 50, 7, 11`, …) — the data-loss half confirmed fixed.

=== SearchBar ===
import { useEffect, useRef, useState } from 'react'
import { useNavigate } from 'react-router-dom'

import { catalogApi } from '@/api/endpoints'
import type { SearchSuggestion } from '@/api/types'
import { formatMoney } from '@/lib/format'

/**
 * Global search with typo tolerance: the backend ranks by trigram similarity, so
 * "eleden ring" still finds Elden Ring. Input is debounced and in-flight
 * requests are aborted on each keystroke.
 */
export function SearchBar({ initialValue = '' }: { initialValue?: string }) {
  const navigate = useNavigate()
  const [term, setTerm] = useState(initialValue)
  const [items, setItems] = useState<SearchSuggestion[]>([])
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false)
  const [active, setActive] = useState(-1)
  const [searching, setSearching] = useState(false)
  const containerRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null)

  useEffect(() => {
    const trimmed = term.trim()
    if (trimmed.length < 2) {
      setItems([])
      setSearching(false)
      return
    }
    const controller = new AbortController()
    setSearching(true)
    const timer = window.setTimeout(() => {
      catalogApi
        .search(trimmed, controller.signal)
        .then((res) => {
          setItems(res.items)
          setOpen(true)
        })
        .catch(() => undefined)
        .finally(() => setSearching(false))
    }, 180)

    return () => {
      window.clearTimeout(timer)
      controller.abort()
    }
  }, [term])

  useEffect(() => {
    function onClickOutside(event: MouseEvent) {
      if (!containerRef.current?.contains(event.target as Node)) setOpen(false)
    }
    document.addEventListener('mousedown', onClickOutside)
    return () => document.removeEventListener('mousedown', onClickOutside)
  }, [])

  function submit(termOverride?: string) {
    const value = (termOverride ?? term).trim()
    setOpen(false)
    if (value) navigate(`/store?q=${encodeURIComponent(value)}`)
  }

  function onKeyDown(event: React.KeyboardEvent<HTMLInputElement>) {
    if (event.key === 'ArrowDown') {
      event.preventDefault()
      setActive((i) => Math.min(i + 1, items.length - 1))
    } else if (event.key === 'ArrowUp') {
      event.preventDefault()
      setActive((i) => Math.max(i - 1, -1))
    } else if (event.key === 'Enter') {
      if (active >= 0 && items[active]) {
        setOpen(false)
        navigate(`/products/${items[active].slug}`)
      } else {
        submit()
      }
    } else if (event.key === 'Escape') {
      setOpen(false)
    }
  }

  return (
    <div ref={containerRef} className="relative w-full">
      <div className="flex items-center gap-2 rounded-full border border-line bg-canvas px-4 py-2.5 focus-within:border-brand-400 focus-within:bg-surface">
        <svg aria-hidden viewBox="0 0 24 24" className="size-4 shrink-0 text-ink-300" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="2">
          <circle cx="11" cy="11" r="7" />
          <path d="m20 20-3.5-3.5" />
        </svg>
        <input
          value={term}
          onChange={(e) => {
            setTerm(e.target.value)
            setActive(-1)
          }}
          onFocus={() => items.length > 0 && setOpen(true)}
          onKeyDown={onKeyDown}
          type="search"
          placeholder="Search games, platforms, regions…"
          aria-label="Search products"
          className="w-full bg-transparent text-sm text-ink-900 placeholder:text-ink-500 focus:outline-none"
        />
        {searching && <span className="size-3.5 animate-spin rounded-full border-2 border-brand-400 border-t-transparent" />}
      </div>

      {open && term.trim().length >= 2 && (
        <div className="absolute inset-x-0 top-full z-50 mt-2 overflow-hidden rounded-card border border-line bg-surface shadow-raised">
          {items.length === 0 ? (
            <p className="px-4 py-5 text-sm text-ink-500">
              No games match “{term.trim()}”. Try a shorter spelling.
            </p>
          ) : (
            <ul>
              {items.map((item, index) => (
                <li key={item.slug}>
                  <button
                    type="button"
                    onMouseEnter={() => setActive(index)}
                    onClick={() => {
                      setOpen(false)
                      navigate(`/products/${item.slug}`)
                    }}
                    className={`flex w-full items-center gap-3 px-3 py-2.5 text-left ${
                      active === index ? 'bg-brand-50' : 'hover:bg-canvas'
                    }`}
                  >
                    <img src={item.coverUrl} alt="" className="h-12 w-9 rounded object-cover" loading="lazy" />
                    <span className="flex-1 text-sm font-medium text-ink-900">{item.title}</span>
                    <span className="text-xs text-ink-300">{Math.round(item.score * 100)}% match</span>
                  </button>
                </li>
              ))}
            </ul>
          )}
          <button
            type="button"
            onClick={() => submit()}
            className="w-full border-t border-line bg-canvas px-4 py-2.5 text-left text-sm font-semibold text-brand-700 hover:bg-brand-50"
          >
            See all results for “{term.trim()}”
          </button>
        </div>
      )}
    </div>
  )
}

export function SearchSummary({ term, total }: { term: string; total: number }) {
  return (
    <p className="text-sm text-ink-500">
      {total} result{total === 1 ? '' : 's'} for <span className="font-semibold text-ink-900">“{term}”</span>
      {total > 0 && <span className="ml-2 text-ink-300">· typo-tolerant matching on</span>}
    </p>
  )
}

export function formatFrom(cents: number) {
  return `from ${formatMoney(cents)}`
}

'eager' : 'lazy'}\n          className=\"size-full object-cover transition duration-300 group-hover:scale-[1.03]\"\n        />\n      </div>\n\n      <div className=\"flex flex-1 flex-col gap-1 p-3\">\n        <p className=\"label-caps truncate text-brand-300\">{product.platforms.map(platformLabel).join(' · ')}</p>\n        <h3 className=\"line-clamp-2 text-sm font-bold leading-snug group-hover:text-accent-300\">\n          {product.title}\n        </h3>\n        <div className=\"mt-auto flex items-baseline gap-1.5 pt-1.5\">\n          <span className=\"font-display text-base font-extrabold text-accent-500\">\n            {formatMoney(product.minPriceCents)}\n          </span>\n          {discount !== null && (\n            <span className=\"text-[0.7rem] text-brand-300 line-through\">{formatMoney(product.maxPriceCents)}</span>\n          )}\n        </div>\n      </div>\n\n      <span className=\"flex items-center justify-between bg-accent-500 px-3 py-2 text-[0.7rem] font-extrabold uppercase tracking-wide text-ink-900 transition group-hover:bg-accent-400\">\n        View offers\n        {product.offerCount > 1 && <span className=\"font-bold\">{product.offerCount}</span>}\n      </span>\n    </Link>\n  )\n}\n\nexport function ProductGrid({ products }: { products: ProductCardType[] }) {\n  return (\n    <div className=\"grid grid-cols-2 gap-3 sm:grid-cols-3 lg:grid-cols-4 xl:grid-cols-5\">\n      {products.map((product) => (\n        <ProductCard key={product.id} product={product} />\n      ))}\n    </div>\n  )\n}\n\nexport function platformLabel(slug: string): string {\n  const labels: Record<string, string> = {\n    steam: 'Steam',\n    playstation: 'PlayStation',\n    xbox: 'Xbox',\n    nintendo: 'Switch',\n    epic: 'Epic',\n    gog: 'GOG',\n  }\n  return labels[slug] ?? slug\n}\n",

[]).find((c) => c.startsWith('kf_session='))\nif (!cookie) {\n  console.log('login failed', login.status)\n  process.exit(1)\n}\nconst jar = cookie.slice('kf_session='.length, cookie.indexOf(';'))\n\nconst res = await fetch(API + '/api/admin/blocks', { headers: { Cookie: `kf_session=${jar}` } })\nconst { blocks } = await res.json()\nconst ordered = [...blocks].sort((a, b) => a.position - b.position || a.id - b.id)\nconsole.log('before:', ordered.map((b) => `${b.position}:${b.type}:${b.key}`).join(' | '))\n\n// Hero stays first; move the category strip to second, keep the rest in order.\nconst hero = ordered.filter((b) => b.type === 'hero')\nconst strip = ordered.filter((b) => b.type === 'category_tiles')\nconst rest = ordered.filter((b) => b.type !== 'hero' && b.type !== 'category_tiles')\nconst target = [...hero, ...strip, ...rest]\n\nfor (const [index, block] of target.entries()) {\n  const position = index + 1\n  if (block.position === position) continue\n  const patch = await fetch(`${API}/api/admin/blocks/${block.id}`, {\n    method: 'PATCH',\n    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', Cookie: `kf_session=${jar}` },\n    body: JSON.stringify({\n      key: block.key,\n      type: block.type,\n      title: block.title,\n      subtitle: block.subtitle,\n      config: block.config ?? {},\n      position,\n      isVisible: block.isVisible,\n      productIds: block.productIds,\n    }),\n  })\n  console.log(`${block.key} -> position ${position}: ${patch.status}`)\n}\n\nconst after = await (await fetch(API + '/api/admin/blocks', { headers: { Cookie: `kf_session=${jar}` } })).json()\nconsole.log('after: ', [...after.blocks].sort((a, b) => a.position - b.position).map((b) => `${b.position}:${b.type}:${b.key}`).join(' | '))\n",

144	## Frontend
145	
146	- `src/api/*` is the only place that touches the network: one typed function per
147	  endpoint, `credentials: 'include'`, error normalisation into `ApiClientError`,
148	  and a small retry for reads that hit a cold-starting free instance.
149	- Context providers for auth and cart; everything else is local state.
150	- The store keeps filters in the URL, so any view is shareable and Back works.
151	- Design tokens (`#4618AC` violet, `#FAD318` CTA yellow) live once in
152	  `src/index.css` under `@theme`; components consume token classes only.
153	
154	## Deployment topology (and the cookie trap)
155	
156	The SPA is on Vercel, the API on Render, the database on Neon. That is three
157	origins, which matters for auth: a cookie set by `*.onrender.com` and read from
158	`*.vercel.app` is a **third-party cookie**, and browsers now block those by
159	default. The symptom is subtle — login returns 200, the UI looks signed in, then
160	every authenticated request is a 401 because the cookie was never stored.
161

Live and verified. Here's what "recreate the theme" actually means in what shipped.

## How I read the reference

I didn't work from memory: I loaded eneba.com in headless Chrome and read its **computed styles**, plus a full-page capture for layout.

| Measured | Value | Where it went |
|---|---|---|
| Brand chrome | `#4618AC` | header, purple bands, active states |
| Deep surface | `#1F0A4D` | product tiles, footer, info panels |
| CTA yellow | `#FAD318` | primary buttons, prices, action bars |
| Mint | `#63E3C2` | positive states, "best price" |
| Corner radius | 0–2px | every card, button, input, badge |
| Type | Metropolis, weights 800 first | `h1` 3.25rem/800, labels 11px/800 uppercase |

## What changed

- **Chrome:** two-row header — logo, white search, `EU · EUR`, cart, `Log in | Register` on row one; a darker catalogue row beneath whose platform links come from `/api/meta`, so the nav reflects what's actually in the catalogue. Footer rebuilt as the dark violet link-column block.
- **Homepage:** full-bleed promo hero with yellow CTA and a featured-price link, purple platform strip with tile + count, then white slices of dark navy tiles (cover, platform caps, title, yellow price, yellow "View offers" bar).
- **Store:** purple catalogue band, sharp bordered filter chips and panel, dark tiles.
- **Product page:** mint-bordered cheapest offer, yellow add-to-cart.
- **Sweep:** all 8–16px radii across 22 files reduced to 2px; circles kept only for spinner, avatar and cart count. Admin and merchant screens inherit the same tokens, so they restyled without per-file work.

## Verified, not assumed

- Deployed to Vercel + Render; **12 live routes render with zero runtime exceptions** (home, store, product, cart, checkout, orders, support, three admin screens, merchant, sign-in).
- Mobile at 390px screenshotted for home and store — header collapses to logo/cart/account plus a full-width search, catalogue row scrolls horizontally.
- Homepage order now runs hero → platform strip → rows. I changed that by patching block **positions** through the admin API in production, not by hardcoding order in React — it stays database-owned, and you can undo it from `/admin/blocks`.

## Assumptions I made (auto mode blocked asking you first)

- **Brand stays "keyforge"** — I borrowed Eneba's design language, not their logo, wordmark art or copy. Their marketing imagery is also not reproduced; the hero uses a block-provided cover image.
- **Metropolis → Figtree.** Metropolis is Eneba's typeface and isn't freely licensed, so I used Figtree from Google Fonts (same geometric skeleton, full 400–900 weight range) with `Metropolis` first in the stack in case you licence it.
- **No fake commerce chrome.** Their "CASHBACK" badges and countdown promo are tied to features you don't have (cashback, campaigns), so I left them out rather than display dead UI.
- **No wishlist/cart-drawer/currency switcher** — the header shows `EU · EUR` as a label, honest about being single-currency.

Now implement acronym matching in both Search and the products list (q filter).

SQL expression for acronym (as a reusable const):
```sql
-- Initialism of the title: "Grand Theft Auto V" -> "gtav", so "gta" and "gtav"
-- both reach the game.
(SELECT string_agg(left(w, 1), '' ORDER BY ord)
   FROM regexp_split_to_table(lower(p.title), '[^a-z0-9]+') WITH ORDINALITY AS t(w, ord)
  WHERE w <> '')
```
Note: `regexp_split_to_table(lower(title), '[^a-z0-9]+')` on "Grand Theft Auto V" → 'grand','theft','auto','v'. With WITH ORDINALITY → alias t(w, ord).

Empty strings: title starting/ending with punctuation yields empty tokens; filter `w <> ''`.

In the products query, the alias for products is `p` (line 92-111 uses p). Let me create const:

```go
// titleAcronym is the initialism of a product title ("Grand Theft Auto V" ->
// "gtav"). Searches compare it by prefix, so "gta", "gtav" and "bg3" all work,
// which plain trigram similarity cannot reach.
const titleAcronym = `(SELECT string_agg(left(w, 1), '' ORDER BY ord)
	FROM regexp_split_to_table(lower(p.title), '[^a-z0-9]+') WITH ORDINALITY AS t(w, ord)
	WHERE w <> '')`
```

Then in Search WHERE add:
`OR ` + titleAcronym + ` LIKE lower(@term) || '%'`

But careful: `@term` used multiple times with different types (text) — all text, fine. Note pgx NamedArgs usage — reuse @term is fine.

Also rank: acronym matches should sort decently. score stays similarity (low ~0.1). With ORDER BY score DESC, an acronym match may rank below other weak matches. For "gta", only one match, fine. For "re" (Resident Evil?) many. Acceptable. But better: add acronym bonus:
`GREATEST(similarity(...), word_similarity(...), CASE WHEN acronym LIKE term||'%' THEN 0.9 ELSE 0 END)`. Hmm computing acronym twice (in SELECT and WHERE). Could use a LATERAL to compute once:

```sql
FROM products p
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT ... AS acronym) acr
```
That's cleaner: compute once, use in both score and WHERE.

Let me restructure Search query with CROSS JOIN LATERAL:

```sql
SELECT p.slug, p.title, p.cover_url,
       GREATEST(similarity(p.title, @term), word_similarity(@term, p.title),
                CASE WHEN acr.acronym LIKE lower(@term) || '%' THEN 0.85 ELSE 0 END) AS score
FROM products p
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT string_agg(...) AS acronym) acr
WHERE p.is_active
  AND EXISTS (...)
  AND (p.title ILIKE '%' || @term || '%'
       OR similarity(p.title, @term) > 0.2
       OR word_similarity(@term, p.title) > 0.5
       OR acr.acronym LIKE lower(@term) || '%')
ORDER BY score DESC, ...

import { createContext, useCallback, useContext, useEffect, useMemo, useState } from 'react'
import type { ReactNode } from 'react'

import { cartApi } from '@/api/endpoints'
import type { Cart } from '@/api/types'
import { useAuth } from '@/features/auth/AuthContext'

type CartState = {
  cart: Cart
  loading: boolean
  error: string | null
  refresh: () => Promise<void>
  add: (offerId: number, quantity?: number) => Promise<void>
  setQuantity: (offerId: number, quantity: number) => Promise<void>
  remove: (offerId: number) => Promise<void>
  clear: () => Promise<void>
}

const emptyCart: Cart = { items: [], itemCount: 0, subtotalCents: 0 }

const CartContext = createContext<CartState | null>(null)

export function CartProvider({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  const { user } = useAuth()
  const [cart, setCart] = useState<Cart>(emptyCart)
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false)
  const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null)

  const refresh = useCallback(async () => {
    if (!user) {
      setCart(emptyCart)
      return
    }
    setLoading(true)
    try {
      setCart(await cartApi.get())
      setError(null)
    } catch (err) {
      setError(err instanceof Error ? err.message : 'Could not load your cart')
    } finally {
      setLoading(false)
    }
  }, [user])

  useEffect(() => {
    void refresh()
  }, [refresh])

  const add = useCallback(async (offerId: number, quantity = 1) => {
    setCart(await cartApi.add(offerId, quantity))
    setError(null)
  }, [])

  const setQuantity = useCallback(async (offerId: number, quantity: number) => {
    setCart(await cartApi.setQuantity(offerId, quantity))
  }, [])

  const remove = useCallback(async (offerId: number) => {
    setCart(await cartApi.remove(offerId))
  }, [])

## The gap: abbreviations didn't search

`gta` is the first thing anyone types, and neither mechanism could reach it — trigrams score "gta" vs "Grand Theft Auto V" almost zero, and `ILIKE '%gta%'` doesn't appear in the title either. Same for `bg3`, `rdr2`, `re4`, `tw3`.

Fix (`backend/internal/repo/catalog.go`): the title's initialism is computed in SQL and compared by prefix, in **both** the suggestion dropdown and the store query.

- `Grand Theft Auto V` → `gtav`, `Red Dead Redemption 2` → `rdr2`, `Resident Evil 4` → `re4`.
- Apostrophes are stripped before tokenising, so `Baldur's Gate 3` → `bg3` instead of the wrong `bsg3` (my first attempt produced exactly that, and the test caught it).
- Acronym hits score 0.9, so an exact abbreviation outranks fuzzy noise.
- No new column, no migration, no backfill — 80 products make the inline computation free.

Verified live after deploy: `gta`/`bg3`/`rdr2`/`re4`/`tw3` all resolve at 0.90, while typos (`eleden ring` @0.64, `cyberpu` @0.88) and full names still work, and store search `q=gta` returns exactly one product. Backend gate green; the DB-backed e2e suite passes.

## What I deliberately did *not* build

- **Guest cart.** Your spec says "sign-in required before payment", and today the cart itself needs auth (401). A guest cart would need offer resolution client-side plus a merge-on-login path — real scope, and the risk sits on the tested purchase flow. Worth it only if you want that reading enforced.
- **Wishlist, password reset.** Not in the PDF; adding them would be breadth over depth, which the brief explicitly discourages.
- **Ticket message threads, auth rate limiting.** Both already recorded in `PROGRESS.md` as accepted limitations.
